messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh Tran was a 31-year-old married judge who had been in his chambers when the earthquake struck his coastal city during the monsoon season. At first it felt like the whole building had taken a single heavy breath, and then the floor lurched hard enough to throw papers from his desk and crack the glass in the windows. He had made it outside with other staff into rain and dust, only to watch part of a nearby apartment block collapse across the street. The sounds of sirens, people shouting, and the wet metallic smell of the street were the last clear pieces before the scene became, in his mind, a series of frightening pictures: a child’s shoe in the mud, a wall falling in sections, a woman reaching into the rubble. When the memory comes back, it does not feel like something that happened years ago; for Minh it arrives all at once, vividly and bodily, with the same smell, the same terror, and the same sense that he is again standing in that broken street.

In the months afterward, certain moments repeatedly pulled him back toward that day. The wail of an ambulance near the courthouse made his stomach drop, and hospital corridors with their antiseptic odor carried him straight into the aftermath of the quake, as if he could already hear the collapse and the cries. He noticed that similar weather was especially hard: when dark clouds gathered and the rain came in sheets, he became tense before he could think, watching the sky with the feeling that something terrible was about to happen again. Those cues did not merely unsettle him; they pushed him into trying hard not to think about the earthquake at all. He would force his attention onto legal briefs, meetings, or television, and when the images broke through anyway he tried to shut them down immediately, because once the pictures started he felt the whole event unfold across his senses and feared he would be overwhelmed by it.

Minh had come to believe that even brief relaxation left him exposed. If he sat quietly on the couch after dinner, or let himself drift while his wife watched television, he found his mind slipping toward the quake, and the sudden vividness of the memory made rest feel dangerous rather than restorative. He stopped allowing himself to unwind, staying busy late into the evening and filling every lull with work or practical tasks. The more the memory arrived in those complete sensory flashes, the more determined he became to keep it at bay, and the harder he pushed it down, the more forcefully it seemed to surface when an ambulance passed, when he walked by a hospital entrance, or when the weather turned stormy. At times he would avoid going out altogether on those days, choosing not to leave home rather than risk encountering the sights and sounds that he knew could set the whole sequence off.

That pattern had begun to narrow his life in ways his wife could see. He declined evening walks, postponed dinners out, and found excuses to work from home when the forecast looked unsettled. At the courthouse he remained composed, but he was increasingly guarded about anything that might make him pause, listen, or remember. In private, he was exhausted by the effort of keeping his thoughts away from the quake, yet he also felt certain that if he let his guard down even briefly, the images would return with their full force and undo the fragile control he had managed to preserve. He had finally sought help because the avoidance was no longer keeping him safe in the way he hoped; it was shrinking his world, straining his marriage, and making every ambulance siren or change in weather feel like a warning. What he most feared was being caught off guard by another surge of that living, sensory memory, and what he most hoped for was to be able to walk outside, hear a siren, or sit quietly with his wife without bracing for the earthquake to come back and take over again.
